hints: Look at what the three paths share. The same maximum height fixes one velocity component for all three; then compare the ranges.
worded:
1. All three paths reach the same maximum height (the dashed line). Height depends only on the vertical launch component, so all three have the same u_y.

2. Time of flight is 2u_y/g, so it is the same for all three: (A) is true.

3. In that same time, C goes farthest, so C has the largest horizontal component: (C) is true.

4. Launch speed is √(u_x² + u_y²). With u_y equal, the largest u_x gives the largest speed, so C is fastest at launch: (B) is true.

5. All three statements hold. (D)
conventional:
Equal maximum heights $H = u_{y}^{2}/2g$ mean equal $u_{y}$ for A, B and C. Hence

$$T = \frac{2u_{y}}{g}\text{ is the same for all three};$$

$$R = u_{x}T\  \Rightarrow \ u_{x} \propto R,\text{ largest for C};\quad\quad u = \sqrt{u_{x}^{2} + u_{y}^{2}}\text{ largest for C}.$$
mistakes: A longer range with the same height does not mean a longer time; the time is set by the height alone.
Read the figure: the common peak height is the key data.
